title: The Pentose Phosphate Pathway: NADPH and Five-Carbon Sugars

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: What two products does the pentose phosphate pathway make that glycolysis never makes, and how much ATP does the pathway itself produce?
cards.back: NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate. It makes no ATP.
cards.why: NADPH is reducing power for biosynthesis and antioxidant defense; ribose-5-phosphate is the sugar every nucleotide is built from.
cards.quote: None of them needs ATP from this pathway, and it makes none.

cards.front: At the glucose-6-phosphate branch point, which enzyme pulls the sugar toward glycolysis, and which pulls it toward the pentose phosphate pathway?
cards.back: Phosphoglucose isomerase pulls toward glycolysis and ATP; glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) pulls toward the pentose phosphate pathway and NADPH.
cards.quote: At glucose-6-phosphate, phosphoglucose isomerase pulls toward glycolysis and ATP; glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase pulls toward the pentose phosphate pathway and NADPH.

cards.front: Why do dividing cells need the pentose phosphate pathway for two separate reasons?
cards.back: Nucleotides are built on ribose, and turning ribonucleotides into DNA building blocks spends NADPH. The pathway supplies both.
cards.quote: Dividing cells need the second road twice over: nucleotides are built on ribose, and turning ribonucleotides into DNA building blocks spends NADPH.

cards.front: Ribose-5-phosphate is the precursor of which activated sugar, required by both purine and pyrimidine synthesis?
cards.back: PRPP.
cards.quote: Ribose-5-phosphate is the precursor of PRPP, the activated sugar that both purine and pyrimidine synthesis require

cards.front: What structural difference lets enzymes tell NAD apart from NADP?
cards.back: One phosphate group. NADP carries an extra phosphate, and that tag is enough for enzymes to discriminate.
cards.quote: NAD and NADP differ by one phosphate group, and that tag is enough for enzymes to tell them apart.

cards.front: In the cytosol the free NAD⁺/NADH pool sits at roughly {{c1::1000:1}} in favor of the oxidized form.
cards.back: Inside mitochondria the NAD pool is far more reduced.
cards.quote: In the cytosol the free NAD⁺/NADH pool sits at roughly 1000:1 in favor of the oxidized form

cards.front: NAD and NADP hold electrons with almost the same strength. What differs between the two cytosolic pools, and how does that suit catabolism versus anabolism?
cards.back: How full each pool is. NAD is kept mostly oxidized, ready to accept electrons from fuel (catabolism). NADP is kept mostly reduced, ready to donate electrons for biosynthesis and glutathione regeneration (anabolism).
cards.quote: Both carriers hold electrons with almost the same strength. What differs is how full each pool is.

cards.front: Suppose a cell's enzymes could not tell NADH from NADPH. What happens to the two pools, and what does the cell lose?
cards.back: Electrons flow from the full NADPH pool to the empty NAD⁺ pool until both sit at the same level. The cell loses both a ready electron acceptor for catabolism and a ready donor for biosynthesis.
cards.why: Rule: keeping the pools apart is what lets breakdown and building run at once.
cards.quote: If enzymes could not tell the two apart, electrons would flow from the full pool to the empty one

cards.front: Take the cytosolic NAD⁺/NADH ratio as 1000:1 and NADP⁺/NADPH as about 1:100. Using RT/2F × ln(ratio of ratios) at 37 °C, how much more reducing is the NADP couple?
cards.back: Ratio of ratios = 1000 ÷ (1/100) = 10⁵. RT/2F ≈ 0.0134 V; ln 10⁵ ≈ 11.5. Product ≈ 154 mV, so the NADP couple is about 150 mV more reducing.
cards.quote: The NADP couple is then about 150 mV more reducing in the cytosol: RT/2F × ln 10⁵ ≈ 154 mV at 37 °C.

cards.front: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting, regulated step of the pentose phosphate pathway, and what does it do?
cards.back: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD). It oxidizes C1 of glucose-6-phosphate to a lactone and reduces the first NADP⁺ to NADPH.
cards.quote: This is the committed, rate-limiting step, and it is the regulated one.

cards.front: Net oxidative phase: G6P + 2 NADP⁺ + H₂O → ribulose-5-P + {{c1::2 NADPH}} + 2 H⁺ + CO₂
cards.back: No ATP is made. The second NADPH and the CO₂ come from 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase.
cards.quote: G6P + 2 NADP⁺ + H₂O → ribulose-5-P + 2 NADPH + 2 H⁺ + CO₂

cards.front: Why does the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway run in only one direction?
cards.back: Each step runs downhill in the cell, the lactone hydrolysis strongly so, and once 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase releases a carbon as CO₂ there is no route back.
cards.quote: Each step runs downhill in the cell, the lactone hydrolysis strongly so, and once the carbon has left as CO₂ there is no route back.

cards.front: What is the main moment-to-moment control on flux through the oxidative phase, and how does it work?
cards.back: NADP⁺ concentration. G6PD is product-inhibited by NADPH, so when NADPH is spent and NADP⁺ rises, inhibition lifts and the pathway speeds up.
cards.quote: G6PD is product-inhibited by NADPH, so the main throttle on the tap is NADP⁺ concentration

cards.front: A red blood cell meets an oxidant drug, and glutathione reductase starts spending NADPH fast. Predict the change in NADP⁺ and in G6PD rate.
cards.back: NADP⁺ rises and G6PD speeds up. Less NADPH means less product inhibition, so the demand itself opens the tap.
cards.quote: NADP⁺ rises as NADPH is spent. Less NADPH means less product inhibition, so G6PD speeds up and the tap opens.

cards.front: Pentose phosphate pathway flux is measured with tracers that follow carbon 1 of glucose. Why is C1 the useful carbon to label?
cards.back: The oxidative phase acts on C1: G6PD oxidizes it, and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase then releases it as CO₂. Following where C1 goes therefore reports flux through the oxidative branch.
cards.quote: Tracers that follow glucose C1 are how PPP flux is actually measured.

cards.front: Why does the pentose phosphate pathway need a reversible sugar exchange in addition to its oxidative phase?
cards.back: The oxidative phase gives a fixed 2 NADPH per five-carbon sugar, and real cells rarely need exactly that ratio. The exchange converts surplus five-carbon sugar to glycolytic sugar, or builds ribose when NADPH is not needed.
cards.quote: The tap's 2-to-1 output is fixed, and real cells rarely need exactly that.

cards.front: Ribulose-5-phosphate is set up for the non-oxidative phase by two routing enzymes. Which makes ribose-5-phosphate, and which makes xylulose-5-phosphate?
cards.back: Phosphopentose isomerase makes ribose-5-phosphate (ketose to aldose, exit toward nucleotides). Phosphopentose epimerase makes xylulose-5-phosphate, an epimer differing only at C3.
cards.quote: Phosphopentose isomerase turns ribulose-5-phosphate into ribose-5-phosphate, the aldose that exits toward nucleotide synthesis.

cards.front: Transketolase runs on {{c1::thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)}}, the same cofactor pyruvate dehydrogenase uses.
cards.back: TPP comes from vitamin B1 (thiamine).
cards.quote: It runs on thiamine pyrophosphate, the same cofactor pyruvate dehydrogenase uses.

cards.front: Transaldolase needs no external cofactor. How does it move its three-carbon unit?
cards.back: An active-site lysine forms a Schiff base with the substrate, the same mechanism aldolase uses in glycolysis.
cards.quote: an active-site lysine forms a Schiff base with the substrate, exactly the mechanism aldolase uses in glycolysis.

cards.front: What is the net reaction of the non-oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway?
cards.back: Three C5 sugars (one ribose-5-P, two xylulose-5-P) ⇌ two fructose-6-P + one glyceraldehyde-3-P. It runs either way.
cards.quote: Net: three C5 sugars (one ribose-5-P and two xylulose-5-P, all made from ribulose-5-P) become two fructose-6-P and one glyceraldehyde-3-P, or the reverse.

cards.front: Check the carbon count of each non-oxidative transfer: transketolase (Xu5P + R5P), transaldolase (S7P + G3P), transketolase again (E4P + Xu5P). Then check the net.
cards.quote: Check the carbons: 3 × 5 = 15, and 2 × 6 + 3 = 15.

cards.front: What decides which direction the non-oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway runs?
cards.back: Nothing has to. Its reactions sit close to equilibrium, so they run toward whichever end is being used up: backward when ribose-5-P is pulled away, forward when surplus five-carbon sugar piles up.
cards.quote: These reactions sit close to equilibrium, so they run toward whichever end is being used up.

cards.front: A patient with chronic alcoholism has thiamine deficiency (Wernicke-Korsakoff). Predict the effect on transketolase, and how that can be used clinically.
cards.back: Transketolase activity falls, because it needs TPP made from thiamine. Assaying transketolase activity is therefore a clinical test of thiamine status.
cards.quote: In thiamine deficiency (Wernicke-Korsakoff, classically in alcoholism) transketolase activity falls — the assay for it is a clinical test of thiamine status.

cards.front: A cell needs 4 NADPH and 2 ribose-5-phosphate. How many glucose-6-phosphate go through the oxidative phase, how much CO₂ is lost, and what does the non-oxidative exchange do?
cards.back: Two G6P through the tap give 4 NADPH, 2 CO₂ and 2 five-carbon sugars, isomerized to 2 ribose-5-P. The exchange is idle: this is the tap's own 2-to-1 ratio (Mode 2).
cards.quote: If the cell wants 2 NADPH for every ribose, the tap alone does the job

cards.front: A dividing cell needs 6 ribose-5-phosphate and makes no NADPH. How many glucose-6-phosphate and ATP does it need, and is any CO₂ lost?
cards.back: 30 carbons needed = 5 G6P; no CO₂. Four become fructose-6-P; one is split by early glycolysis into 2 glyceraldehyde-3-P (1 ATP at PFK-1). The exchange runs backward twice: 4 C6 + 2 C3 → 6 C5.
cards.quote: Net: 5 glucose-6-phosphate + 1 ATP → 6 ribose-5-phosphate.

cards.front: Six glucose-6-phosphate go through the oxidative phase, and all the five-carbon sugar is recycled back to glucose-6-phosphate. How many NADPH and CO₂ come out, and how many G6P return?
cards.back: Tap: 6 × 2 = 12 NADPH, 6 CO₂, six C5 (30 C). Exchange: 4 F6P + 2 G3P; the two G3P join into a fifth hexose, so 5 G6P return. Net: 1 G6P → 6 CO₂ + 12 NADPH, the most one glucose can give.
cards.quote: Net: one whole glucose-6-phosphate is taken apart into 6 CO₂, and the cell collects 12 NADPH.

cards.front: A cell needs NADPH and ATP. Three glucose-6-phosphate go through the oxidative phase and the leftover sugars go down glycolysis. Tally NADPH, CO₂, pyruvate, NADH and net ATP.
cards.back: 6 NADPH and 3 CO₂. Three C5 → 2 F6P + 1 G3P = 5 three-carbon sugars, giving 5 pyruvate, 5 NADH and 10 ATP; PFK-1 spends 2 splitting the F6P, so net 8 ATP. The ATP is glycolysis's, not the PPP's.
cards.quote: Three glucose-6-phosphate give 6 NADPH and 3 CO₂, and their leftover sugars give 5 pyruvate, 5 NADH and a net 8 ATP

cards.front: A red blood cell under oxidant attack needs only NADPH, but it has no gluconeogenesis. Predict what it does with the fructose-6-P and glyceraldehyde-3-P the exchange makes, and which modes this blends.
cards.back: Fructose-6-P returns to the tap (via glucose-6-P); glyceraldehyde-3-P cannot be rebuilt into hexose, so it goes down glycolysis. A blend of Mode 3 (recycle for NADPH) and Mode 4 (into glycolysis).
cards.why: Rule: full recycling (Mode 3) needs gluconeogenic enzymes to rejoin the three-carbon sugars.
cards.quote: it has no gluconeogenesis: it returns its fructose-6-phosphate to the tap and sends the three-carbon sugar down glycolysis, a blend of Modes 3 and 4.

cards.front: A cell needs 10 NADPH and 2 ribose-5-phosphate. How many times does the oxidative phase run, and how many forward turns of the exchange are needed?
cards.back: Tap runs n/2 = 5 times, giving 5 C5. Exchange forward (n/2 − r)/3 = (5 − 2)/3 = 1 turn: 2 C5 kept as ribose, 3 C5 → 2 F6P + 1 G3P.
cards.why: Zero exchange only when n = 2r; a negative answer means it runs backward.
cards.quote: the tap must run n/2 times, and the exchange must run forward by (n/2 − r)/3 turns.

cards.front: A liver cell making fat runs the oxidative phase hard and needs almost no ribose. A drug blocks transketolase. Predict what happens to its five-carbon sugars and its NADPH supply per glucose.
cards.back: Five-carbon sugars pile up, because they cannot be turned back into glycolytic sugar and recycled. Without recycling, each G6P yields only 2 NADPH, not the up-to-12 of Mode 3.
cards.why: Rule: the reversible exchange clears surplus C5 so it can return to the tap.
cards.quote: It has to be turned back into glycolytic sugar, or it piles up.

cards.front: A dividing lymphocyte already has abundant NADPH and needs ribose fast. A transketolase inhibitor is added. Predict its ribose supply.
cards.back: Ribose supply falls. High NADPH holds G6PD nearly shut, so ribose must come from the exchange run backward from fructose-6-P and glyceraldehyde-3-P, and that route needs transketolase.
cards.why: Rule: Mode 1 depends entirely on the reversible exchange.
cards.quote: The ribose has to come from the exchange run backward, out of fructose-6-P and glyceraldehyde-3-P pulled from glycolysis.

cards.front: The oxidative phase releases CO₂ without consuming O₂. Does heavy pentose phosphate pathway flux raise the body's respiratory quotient (CO₂ out / O₂ in)? What does an RQ above 1 signal?
cards.back: Not by itself: the NADPH is later spent on oxygen-using reactions or on building fat. An RQ above 1 signals net fat synthesis, which spends PPP NADPH.
cards.quote: An RQ above 1 signals net fat synthesis, which spends PPP NADPH.
cards.section: Why the oxidative phase does not raise the respiratory quotient

cards.front: What is glutathione, structurally, and what is its role?
cards.back: A tripeptide (γ-Glu-Cys-Gly) with a reactive cysteine thiol; the cell's frontline antioxidant.
cards.quote: Glutathione is a small tripeptide (γ-Glu-Cys-Gly) with a reactive cysteine thiol, and it is the cell's frontline antioxidant.
cards.section: The red cell: when the tap breaks

cards.front: How does the glutathione cycle link peroxide removal to NADPH?
cards.back: Glutathione peroxidase spends GSH to neutralize peroxides, making GSSG. Glutathione reductase spends NADPH to turn GSSG back into GSH.
cards.quote: glutathione reductase then spends NADPH to turn GSSG back into GSH.
cards.section: The red cell: when the tap breaks

cards.front: Why are mature red blood cells especially dependent on the pentose phosphate pathway?
cards.back: They have no nucleus and no mitochondria, need little ribose, and get their NADPH mainly from the PPP, so their whole glutathione cycle leans on G6PD.
cards.quote: A mature red blood cell needs little ribose, has no nucleus and no mitochondria, and gets its NADPH mainly from the PPP
cards.section: The red cell: when the tap breaks

cards.front: A man with G6PD deficiency eats fava beans. Trace the cascade from the enzyme to the clinical outcome.
cards.back: G6PD↓ → NADPH↓ → GSH↓ → reactive oxygen accumulates → hemoglobin oxidizes and clumps into Heinz bodies → cells burst in the circulation or are removed by the spleen → hemolytic crisis.
cards.quote: The cascade: G6PD↓ → NADPH↓ → GSH↓ → reactive oxygen accumulates → hemoglobin oxidizes and clumps into Heinz bodies
cards.section: The red cell: when the tap breaks

cards.front: In a G6PD-deficient red cell, NADP⁺ rises under oxidant stress just as in a normal cell. Why can't the cell compensate?
cards.back: The signal is there, but there is too little working G6PD to answer it. With no nucleus, the red cell cannot transcribe more enzyme, and it has little else to fall back on.
cards.quote: A red cell has no nucleus, so it cannot transcribe more enzyme, and it has little else to fall back on.
cards.section: The red cell: when the tap breaks

cards.front: G6PD deficiency affects roughly 400 million people. Why are males affected more often?
cards.back: The G6PD gene is on the X chromosome. Its many variants differ in severity.
cards.quote: The gene is on the X chromosome, so males are affected more often, and its many variants differ in severity.
cards.section: The red cell: when the tap breaks

cards.front: If G6PD deficiency can cause hemolytic crises, why is the allele so common?
cards.back: It is thought to persist because deficient red cells seem a poorer home for Plasmodium falciparum; prevalence broadly overlaps historical malaria. A balanced polymorphism, like sickle-cell trait, though protection strength varies between studies.
cards.quote: It is a balanced polymorphism, the textbook companion to sickle-cell trait
cards.section: The red cell: when the tap breaks

cards.front: Many dividing tumor cells run both glycolysis (the Warburg effect) and the pentose phosphate pathway hard. Why the PPP?
cards.back: They need NADPH for lipid and nucleotide synthesis and for surviving their own oxidative stress.
cards.quote: because they need NADPH for lipid and nucleotide synthesis and for surviving their own oxidative stress

cards.front: Name other NADPH sources besides the pentose phosphate pathway, and explain why the red cell, not the liver, is the cleaner example of a pure PPP-NADPH demand.
cards.back: Malic enzyme, isocitrate dehydrogenase and folate metabolism. Liver and fat making fatty acids get a substantial share of NADPH from malic enzyme, while the red cell relies mainly on the PPP.
cards.quote: which is why the red cell is the cleaner example of an NADPH-only demand

cards.front: A tumor loses p53 function. Predict the direct effect on G6PD, and why the net effect on the pathway is not certain.
cards.back: p53 can restrain G6PD by binding it and blocking its assembly into the active dimer, so loss of p53 can take that brake off. But p53 also induces TIGAR, which can push glucose into the PPP, so the net effect depends on the cell.
cards.quote: The tumor suppressor p53 can restrain G6PD by binding it and blocking its assembly into the active dimer.
cards.section: Long-term control of G6PD, and how p53 acts
